items.title: Hypolite Charles Interview, 1963-04-13
items.q: I played over there because you were in a roof garden for a whole summer, for Mr. Ballantyne. Sure. He came and got me

ctx.x: those places from that day on. Tell me, did you notice in the people that you associated with sort of an attitude of looking down their nose at you because you were a jazz player, did you meet any of that at all in New Orleans? Well that's good. I'm glad they didn't. I know in North Louisiana, how I was raised in a very strict Protestant atmosphere. All of this was looked upon as being highly sinful and so on, you know. And so we had to skirt around the edge of jazz for a long

time, you know. You're from around Shreveport? Yes, north of Shreveport. Well, I played over there because you were in a roof garden for a whole summer, for Mr. Ballantyne. Sure. He came and got me, I was playing that tomass in there. That's right. That's right. A whole summer I played that. Oh but that was one of the best roof garden jobs I ever had. Oh that was a nice place. Oh, we used to live at Dr. King's house on Douglas Street. I used to go to, on Sundays I used to go to the Protestant church. They had a…

people there. Oh, in those days there were relatively few Catholics there. That's right. That's right. Did they have any jazzy piano playing and jazzy music at the Protestant church you attended? No. Well I was raised up, for instance, going to both white churches and also Negro churches up there. They had some very gut-buckety piano playing, you know, rather goofy piano playing in the churches.
